funFacts.fact: Adrenaline (epinephrine) was first used in cardiac arrest in 1906, but it wasn't until the 1960s that it became a standard part of CPR protocols.
Ventricular fibrillation is the most common initial rhythm in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but survival rates drop by roughly 10% for every minute defibrillation is delayed.
The first documented use of mouth-to-mouth ventilation was by the biblical Elisha around 800 BC. Modern CPR wasn't developed until 1960.
The human body contains roughly 60,000 miles of blood vessels — enough to wrap around the Earth more than twice.

Atropine was removed from the cardiac arrest algorithm in 2010 (ILCOR) after evidence showed no benefit for pulseless electrical activity or asystole. It remains essential for symptomatic bradycardia and organophosphate poisoning.
The LUCAS mechanical chest compression device delivers exactly 102 compressions per minute and 5 cm depth — perfectly consistent, every time. But manual CPR quality varies widely between providers.

In tension pneumothorax, mediastinal shift compresses the contralateral lung AND kinks the vena cava — it's the venous return obstruction, not just the lung collapse, that causes cardiovascular collapse.
Glucagon can be used to treat severe beta-blocker overdose because it activates adenylate cyclase through a separate receptor, bypassing the blocked beta receptors entirely.

The cricothyroid membrane averages 10mm tall and 9mm wide in adults — just large enough for a 6mm tube. It's the narrowest point of access to the airway but the most reliable in a 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' scenario.
The earliest recorded ambulance service was operated by the Order of St John in Jerusalem during the First Crusade (1099), using carts to transport wounded knights to treatment tents.

Naloxone has a shorter half-life (30–90 minutes) than most opioids. Patients who receive naloxone for opioid overdose can re-sedate after it wears off — hence the need for observation or extended-release formulations.

The Kussmaul breathing pattern (deep, rapid respirations) seen in diabetic ketoacidosis is the body's attempt to blow off CO2 and compensate for metabolic acidosis — it's respiratory compensation for a metabolic problem.
The QT interval should be less than half the R-R interval at normal heart rates. A corrected QT (QTc) > 500ms significantly increases the risk of torsades de pointes.
Modern paramedic practice traces its origins to the 'Freedom House' ambulance service in Pittsburgh (1967), which trained unemployed Black men as the first paramedics in the United States.
Intranasal fentanyl achieves effective plasma concentrations within 10 minutes and avoids the need for IV access — making it a game-changer for pain management in paediatric and burn patients.

Neurogenic shock (loss of sympathetic tone after spinal cord injury above T6) causes hypotension with bradycardia — the opposite of hypovolaemic shock, where tachycardia is the expected compensatory response.
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left — which is why endobronchial intubation and aspiration preferentially affect the right lung.

Therapeutic hypothermia (now called Targeted Temperature Management) was inspired by cases in the 1950s, but the landmark 2002 HACA trial was what convinced the resuscitation community to adopt it routinely.
Amiodarone contains roughly 75mg of iodine per 200mg dose — about 37% iodine by weight. A single loading dose can cause both hyper- and hypothyroidism in susceptible patients.

The Star of Life symbol used on ambulances worldwide was designed by the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration in 1973. The six points represent detection, reporting, response, on-scene care, care in transit, and transfer to definitive care.

In anaphylaxis, massive vasodilation can increase vascular capacity by up to 30%, effectively creating a 'relative hypovolaemia' — which is why adrenaline (a vasoconstrictor) is the definitive treatment, not just fluid alone.
Wellens' syndrome (biphasic or deeply inverted T waves in V2-V3) indicates critical proximal LAD stenosis. These patients need urgent cath lab referral — stress testing can be fatal.

Adrenaline in anaphylaxis works within seconds via the IM route because it's absorbed into the vast capillary network of muscle. Subcutaneous injection is slower and less effective — hence the recommendation for IM injection into the anterolateral thigh.

The epidural space contains fat, veins, and lymphatics — it's the target for epidural analgesia. The subarachnoid space contains CSF and is the target for spinal anaesthesia. The difference is one membrane: the dura mater.

In the PARAMEDIC2 trial, adrenaline improved survival to hospital discharge from 3.2% to 8.0% in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest — but survivors had higher rates of severe neurological impairment compared to placebo.

The average time from 000 call to ambulance arrival in urban Australia is approximately 8–10 minutes. In rural and remote areas, it can exceed 30 minutes — which is why community first-responder programs are critical.

Ketamine is a 'dissociative' anaesthetic — it doesn't suppress the respiratory drive or gag reflex at typical doses, making it one of the safest induction agents for RSI in the prehospital environment.

In hypovolaemic shock, the body sacrifices skin, kidneys, and gut perfusion to maintain coronary and cerebral blood flow. By the time hypotension appears (class III shock), the patient has already lost 30–40% of their blood volume.

Sgarbossa criteria (concordant ST elevation ≥1mm, concordant ST depression ≥1mm in V1-V3, or discordant STE ≥5mm) help diagnose MI in the presence of LBBB — a scenario where standard STEMI criteria don't apply.

Helicopter EMS typically cruising at 120–150 knots can reduce transport times significantly, but tasking criteria matter — studies show HEMS benefit is greatest for time-critical conditions like trauma and STEMI where ground transport exceeds 30 minutes.

The 'dose' column on a drug card isn't just a suggestion — adrenaline 1:1000 is 1mg/mL (for IM/SC), while adrenaline 1:10000 is 0.1mg/mL (for IV). Confusing the two has caused fatal intracerebral haemorrhage.

The Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations) is a late sign of raised intracranial pressure. By the time you see it, herniation may already be underway — it's a pre-terminal sign.

The femoral artery pulse is palpable at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament — in cardiac arrest, it's the recommended site for pulse checks because central pulses persist longer than peripheral ones.

The 'three-phase' model of cardiac arrest describes: the electrical phase (0–4 min, defibrillation most effective), the circulatory phase (4–10 min, CPR before defibrillation improves outcomes), and the metabolic phase (>10 min, poor prognosis).

Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) relieves angina by venodilation (reducing preload) more than arterial dilation. It doesn't 'open blocked arteries' — it reduces the heart's workload, lowering myocardial oxygen demand.

The introduction of paramedic practitioners in the UK demonstrated that paramedics trained in alternate care pathways can safely manage many patients without transport — reducing ED burden by up to 50% in some trial cohorts.

In acute mountain sickness and high-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE), cerebral vasodilation from hypoxia increases intracranial pressure. Diamox (acetazolamide) works by inducing a metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation.

The left anterior descending (LAD) artery supplies roughly 50% of the left ventricle's myocardium. Occlusion proximal to the first septal branch is why anterior STEMIs carry such high mortality — it's a massive territory at risk.

Metaraminol is a pure alpha-agonist used as a vasopressor in Australia. Unlike noradrenaline, it doesn't require a central line and can be given via peripheral IV — but its longer onset means you need to anticipate hypotension, not react to it.

The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) innervates the diaphragm — 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.' A spinal cord injury above C3 paralyses the diaphragm, making these patients immediately ventilator-dependent.

The 'log roll' technique was standard for spinal immobilisation for decades, but recent evidence suggests that manual in-line stabilisation with scoop stretchers causes less spinal movement during extrication.

Rhabdomyolysis from crush injury releases myoglobin, which clogs renal tubules and causes acute kidney injury. The 'crush syndrome' triad is: hypovolaemia, hyperkalaemia, and myoglobinuria — early aggressive fluid resuscitation is the key intervention.

Ondansetron (Zofran) works by blocking 5-HT3 serotonin receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and GI tract. It revolutionised antiemetic therapy because it doesn't cause the sedation or dystonic reactions of older agents like metoclopramide.

In Australia, paramedics are regulated under the National Registration and Accreditation Scheme (NRAS) by the Paramedicine Board of Australia since 2018 — making paramedicine a nationally regulated health profession.

The P-wave represents atrial depolarisation, but the left atrium depolarises slightly after the right. A notched or wide P-wave ('P mitrale') suggests left atrial enlargement, often from mitral valve disease.

Sodium bicarbonate in tricyclic antidepressant overdose works by alkalinising the serum, which reduces the fraction of free drug that binds to cardiac sodium channels — reversing the wide QRS and arrhythmias within minutes.

The Fick principle states that cardiac output equals oxygen consumption divided by the arteriovenous oxygen difference. It's the physiological basis for why increasing heart rate and stroke volume are the only ways to boost oxygen delivery.

The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humerus — mid-shaft humeral fractures commonly injure it, causing wrist drop. Always test wrist extension before and after immobilising a humeral fracture.

In traumatic cardiac arrest, the priority sequence is different: address reversible causes (hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade) before or alongside CPR — standard ALS algorithms alone have near-zero survival in this context.

Midazolam is water-soluble at acidic pH but becomes lipophilic at physiological pH — which is why it crosses the blood-brain barrier so quickly after injection. This also makes it the fastest-onset benzodiazepine for seizure termination.

The earliest documented 'ambulance' was a horse-drawn wagon used by Spanish military forces in the 1480s during the siege of Málaga. The word 'ambulance' comes from the Latin 'ambulare' — to walk or move.

In sepsis, the 'cytokine storm' causes both vasodilation AND increased capillary permeability. Fluid leaks into the interstitial space ('third spacing'), which is why septic patients can be oedematous yet intravascularly depleted simultaneously.

Atrial fibrillation causes stasis of blood in the left atrial appendage, forming thrombus. The risk of stroke in AF is quantified by the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score — patients scoring ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women) generally need anticoagulation.

Ipratropium bromide is an anticholinergic bronchodilator derived from atropine but modified to be poorly absorbed systemically — so it relaxes airway smooth muscle without the tachycardia, dry mouth, and blurred vision of systemic atropine.

CPR generates only about 20–30% of normal cardiac output. 'CCR' (cardiocerebral resuscitation) — continuous compressions without ventilations for the first few minutes of witnessed VF arrest — may improve cerebral perfusion compared to traditional 30:2 CPR.

The 'lethal triad' of trauma is hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy — each worsens the others in a vicious cycle. This is why trauma protocols emphasise warm fluids, early haemorrhage control, and damage control surgery.

Magnesium sulphate is the first-line treatment for eclamptic seizures — not benzodiazepines. It works by antagonising calcium at NMDA receptors and causing cerebral vasodilation, reducing seizure risk by over 50% compared to diazepam.

Australian 'flight paramedics' and 'rescue paramedics' undergo additional training in aeromedical retrieval, winch operations, and wilderness medicine. In NSW alone, aeromedical services respond to over 7,000 missions annually.

Brugada syndrome is a genetic sodium channelopathy that causes VF and sudden cardiac death in young, otherwise healthy individuals. The classic ECG shows a 'pseudo-RBBB' pattern with coved ST elevation in V1-V3.

Adenosine has a half-life of less than 10 seconds in the blood — it's rapidly degraded by adenosine deaminase on red blood cells. This is why it must be given as a rapid bolus through a large-bore proximal IV, followed immediately by a saline flush.

In spinal shock (loss of all cord function below a lesion), there is flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and loss of sensation. Reflexes typically return within 24–72 hours, and the return of the bulbocavernosus reflex marks the end of spinal shock.

The carotid sinus baroreceptors at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery respond to stretch. Carotid sinus massage increases vagal tone, slowing AV node conduction — useful for terminating SVT, but risky in patients with carotid stenosis.
ECMO initiated during cardiac arrest (ECPR) has shown survival rates of 30–50% in selected patients in specialised centres — dramatically higher than conventional CPR for refractory VF/VT.

Calcium chloride contains three times more bioavailable calcium ions per gram than calcium gluconate. For immediate correction of hyperkalaemia-induced arrhythmias, calcium chloride is preferred — but it must be given via a central or large-bore peripheral line.

The concept of the 'golden hour' — that trauma patients have the best outcomes if they reach definitive care within 60 minutes — was coined by R Adams Cowley in the 1960s. Modern evidence suggests it's actually the 'golden minutes' for haemorrhaging patients.

The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve shifts right (releasing more O₂ to tissues) with increased temperature, acidosis, increased PaCO₂, and increased 2,3-DPG. Active tissues produce all of these — a beautiful self-regulating system.

De Winter T-waves (upsloping ST depression with tall, peaked T waves in V1-V6) are a STEMI equivalent indicating acute proximal LAD occlusion. They appear in about 2% of acute LAD occlusions and are frequently missed.

Tranexamic acid (TXA) works by blocking the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, preventing clot breakdown. The CRASH-2 trial showed it reduces mortality from trauma haemorrhage — but only if given within 3 hours of injury.

The recurrent laryngeal nerve on the left hooks under the aortic arch, while the right hooks under the subclavian artery. This makes the left nerve vulnerable to compression by aortic aneurysms or mediastinal masses, causing hoarseness.

End-tidal CO₂ (ETCO₂) is a real-time indicator of cardiac output during CPR. An ETCO₂ < 10 mmHg after 20 minutes of resuscitation strongly predicts non-survival — it's the most reliable prognostic indicator available during an arrest.

In status epilepticus, the longer the seizure continues, the harder it is to terminate — GABA receptors internalise and glutamate receptors proliferate, making the brain progressively more excitable. This is why early benzodiazepine administration is critical.

Salbutamol causes hypokalaemia by stimulating Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, driving potassium into cells. Repeated nebulised doses in asthma exacerbations can drop serum potassium to dangerous levels — always monitor if giving multiple doses.
The first documented use of a defibrillator on a human was in 1947 by Claude Beck during open-chest surgery on a 14-year-old boy. Closed-chest defibrillation wasn't developed until 1956.

The J-wave (Osborn wave) appears as a notch at the J-point in hypothermia, hypercalcaemia, and some genetic conditions. In hypothermia, its size roughly correlates with the degree of core temperature depression.

Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine sedation by competitively blocking the GABA-A receptor's benzodiazepine binding site. In chronic benzodiazepine users, it can precipitate seizures — which is why it's used cautiously in the prehospital setting.

Aortic dissection type A (involving the ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency with mortality increasing 1–2% per hour. Type B (descending only) is usually managed medically unless complicated by rupture or malperfusion.

The 'chain of survival' concept was introduced by the American Heart Association in 1991: early access, early CPR, early defibrillation, early advanced care. A fifth link — post-cardiac arrest care — was added in 2010.

Droperidol was black-boxed by the FDA in 2001 due to concerns about QT prolongation — but the doses implicated were far higher than the 1.25–2.5mg used for nausea and agitation in emergency settings. Many toxicologists argue the warning was an overreaction.

In Australia, the emergency number 000 was introduced in 1961. Before that, people dialled their local police, fire, or ambulance station directly. The 000 number was chosen because '0' was the easiest digit to dial on a rotary phone in the dark.

Pulse pressure (systolic minus diastolic) narrows in cardiac tamponade because pericardial fluid limits diastolic filling, dropping stroke volume while compensatory vasoconstriction raises diastolic pressure. A PP < 25 mmHg is a red flag.

Electrical alternans (beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude) on ECG is a classic sign of pericardial effusion — the heart literally swings back and forth in a fluid-filled pericardial sac with each beat.

Paracetamol's mechanism is still debated but likely involves COX inhibition in the CNS where peroxide tone is low. This selectivity is why paracetamol reduces pain and fever without GI side effects — unlike traditional NSAIDs.

Double sequential defibrillation (two defibrillators firing simultaneously) has been used for refractory VF, but the 2023 PARAMEDIC-DS trial found no survival benefit — it's no longer recommended in routine practice.

In burns, the 'rule of nines' only applies to adults. In children, the head is proportionally larger (up to 18% in infants) and the legs smaller — use the Lund-Browder chart for accurate paediatric burn surface area estimation.

Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) for cyanide poisoning turns the patient's skin and urine bright red — a vivid but harmless side effect. It works by directly binding cyanide to form cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12), which is renally excreted.

The NSW Ambulance Special Operations Team includes paramedics trained in urban search and rescue, hazardous materials, and tactical medicine. They were deployed extensively during the 2019–2020 Black Summer bushfires.

Takotsubo cardiomyopathy ('broken heart syndrome') mimics STEMI with ST elevation and troponin rise, but coronary arteries are clean. The apex balloons out due to catecholamine-mediated stunning — typically triggered by severe emotional stress.

Hyperkalaemia causes peaked T-waves, widened QRS, and eventually a sine-wave pattern leading to asystole. In the kidney failure patient who misses dialysis, a K⁺ > 6.5 mmol/L is a 'treat now before ECG changes worsen' emergency.

Ethanol and methanol are both metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase, but methanol produces formic acid — the toxin that causes blindness. Fomepizole (or ethanol itself) blocks this enzyme, giving the kidneys time to excrete methanol unchanged.

The Circle of Willis provides collateral cerebral circulation — but it's anatomically complete in only about 20% of people. In the remaining 80%, variations mean some brain regions have less collateral protection against arterial occlusion.
In traumatic cardiac arrest from penetrating trauma, a resuscitative thoracotomy can have survival rates up to 20% — but only if the patient had signs of life at some point during transport.

The Bohr effect describes how increased CO₂ (and decreased pH) in active tissues reduces haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, causing more O₂ release exactly where it's needed most. It's one of the body's most elegant feedback loops.

Rocuronium is increasingly preferred over suxamethonium for RSI because it has fewer contraindications (no hyperkalaemia risk in burns/crush/neurological injury). Sugammadex can reverse it — but isn't yet widely available in Australian prehospital care.

The left main coronary artery is sometimes called the 'widow-maker' because occlusion causes massive anterior and lateral wall infarction. ECG shows widespread ST elevation across most leads with reciprocal changes inferiorly.

The first paramedic program in Australia was established at Charles Sturt University in 1995. Before that, ambulance officers were trained through in-service apprenticeship models rather than university degrees.

papers.title: Health and Medical Preparedness and Response to the 2024 Republican National Convention
papers.summary: This case report describes comprehensive health and medical planning and multi-agency response for a large-scale national political convention, providing a template for mass gathering EMS preparedness.

papers.title: The role of freeze-dried plasma in a world of whole blood: a Canadian prehospital and transport perspective
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: This commentary argues freeze-dried plasma complements whole blood in prehospital resuscitation, offering a scalable, shelf-stable solution for rural and remote regions with long transport times.

papers.title: Duration of Emergency Medical Services-Initiated Prehospital Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Efforts and Survival for Pediatric Patients with Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
papers.summary: This nationwide cohort study examined whether longer prehospital CPR duration affects survival in paediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, finding that prolonged CPR efforts can still yield favourable neurological outcomes in selected patients.

papers.title: Geographic Inequalities in Prehospital Critical Care for Cardiac Arrest: A Spatial Analysis of Deprivation and Service Configuration
papers.summary: This spatial analysis examined how deprivation levels and prehospital critical care service configuration affect cardiac arrest outcomes, revealing persistent geographic disparities in access and survival.

papers.title: Airway Management Skills and Devices on Italian Helicopter Emergency Medical Service: A National Survey
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: This national survey documented airway management skills and device availability across Italian HEMS services, showing variability in advanced airway training and device adoption.

papers.title: Factors associated with hospital transport in emergency medical services-attended out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.summary: Retrospective cohort of 3339 OHCA patients found 68.9% were not transported, with transport more likely in witnessed arrests, bystander CPR, hypertension, and shorter time from last known normal, and less likely with older age, malignancy, prior stroke, and arrests at home.

papers.title: Feasibility and agreement of a self-adhesive EEG electrode set versus conventional EEG in postanoxic coma
papers.summary: Comparison of forehead EEG electrodes versus conventional EEG in 51 postanoxic coma patients found forehead recordings were interpretable in 74.1% of cases with moderate agreement, suggesting potential as a screening tool to reduce technician workload.

papers.title: Emergency Medicine Residents in the Prehospital Setting: Does This Augment Training?
papers.summary: Five-year retrospective of a physician response vehicle staffed by EM residents found residents gained valuable exposure to adult and paediatric cardiac arrests, refusals, death pronouncements, and critical trauma, with an average of 28-79 encounters per resident.

papers.title: Utilization and Metrics Associated with Paramedic Treat and Discharge Medical Directives for Paramedic Services and Emergency Departments: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.summary: This retrospective cohort study analysed paramedic treat and discharge medical directives to understand utilisation patterns and key metrics for prehospital and emergency department decision-making — the findings provide valuable insights into the scope, safety, and operational impact of treat-and-refer pathways.

papers.title: Can a Large Language Model Grounded in Text-Based Agency-Specific Prehospital Protocols Provide Accurate Care Recommendations?
papers.summary: This study tested whether a large language model trained on agency-specific prehospital protocol documents could generate accurate care recommendations — they found promising accuracy for protocol interpretation and clinical decision support, suggesting potential for LLMs to assist with guideline navigation at the point of care.

papers.title: Predictive Value of Carotid Artery Doppler Ultrasound for Resuscitation Outcomes in Patients with Cardiac Arrest
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine

papers.title: Evaluation of a Situational Judgment Test for Paramedic Student Selection
papers.summary: This study validated a situational judgement test for selecting paramedic students, finding it effectively assessed non-technical skills and predicted suitability for paramedic training.

papers.title: Eye-related emergency calls and prehospital management in region Zealand, Danmark: a register-based cohort study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Register-based cohort of 340 eye-related emergency calls found chemical exposures (31.5%), vision loss (25.9%), and trauma (18.2%) as leading causes, with 11.5% of patients initially coded for eye problems later diagnosed with stroke.

papers.title: Prophylaxis of opioid-induced nausea in helicopter emergency medical service: a prospective quasi-experimental study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Prospective study of 205 HEMS patients comparing ondansetron prophylaxis, aromatherapy, and no prophylaxis for opioid-induced nausea — neither intervention showed benefit compared to no prophylaxis in unselected patients.

papers.title: Intranasal Versus Intramuscular Midazolam in Pediatric Seizure Control: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.summary: Meta-analysis testing whether intranasal or intramuscular midazolam works better for paediatric seizures without cannula access — intramuscular midazolam was associated with faster seizure termination and less need for rescue therapy, especially in the prehospital setting.

papers.title: Manual versus Automated Ventilation with an i-gel® Airway During Short-Haul Helicopter Operations
papers.summary: Simulation study comparing bag-valve ventilation with automated ventilation during short-haul helicopter rescue using an i-gel — automated ventilation achieved target minute ventilation more consistently, caused less airway movement, and avoided disconnects.

papers.title: The role of tactical police medics in the prehospital environment: results from an interview study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Interview study exploring how Swedish tactical police medics view their training, role, and real-world practice — they reported being well trained but underused, with scope restrictions and inconsistent collaboration limiting what they can actually do.

papers.title: Paramedics' decisions to withhold resuscitation in traumatic cardiac arrest: accuracy of paramedic assessments compared with autopsy findings
papers.summary: Retrospective Ontario review testing how paramedics decide to withhold CPR in traumatic cardiac arrest — most no-CPR decisions were based on signs clearly incompatible with life, and post-mortem findings supported paramedic assessment in the large majority of cases.

papers.title: The impact of advanced pre-hospital interventions on scene time
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Retrospective physician-led HEMS trauma study examining whether more advanced interventions are stretching scene times — each additional intervention increased scene time by 41%, although overall scene times stayed similar over two decades because of changing case mix.

papers.title: Out-of-Hospital Management of Suspected Spinal Cord Injuries: How Much Evidence Does it Take to Change Practice?
papers.summary: Commentary challenging continued routine spinal immobilisation in suspected spinal injury — the authors argue decades of evidence now consistently show harm without benefit, and that paramedic scope should evolve to reflect current evidence.

papers.title: Early Intensive Blood Pressure Reduction After Intracerebral Hemorrhage Is Associated With Worse Functional Outcome: The Risk of Overshooting Blood Pressure Goals
papers.summary: Retrospective cohort testing whether rapid systolic BP reduction ≤150 mm Hg after spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage improved outcomes — early target achievement and overshooting <120 mm Hg were associated with worse functional outcome.

papers.title: No delayed intracranial hemorrhage in head injury patients on oral anticoagulants and with normal CT: a retrospective study of 215 patients
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Retrospective review tested whether immediate discharge after normal CT was safe for anticoagulated head-injury patients with GCS 14–15 — no delayed intracranial haemorrhage, neurosurgical intervention, or clinically significant deterioration occurred.

papers.title: Comparison of needle decompression to simple (finger) thoracostomy in non-perfused cadaveric models with theoretical tension pneumothorax
papers.summary: Cadaveric crossover study testing needle decompression versus simple thoracostomy for theoretical tension pneumothorax — simple thoracostomy was more successful and faster, but the model limits clinical certainty.

papers.title: Healthcare costs of expedited transport compared with standard care following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: results from the EVIDENCE randomised controlled trial
papers.summary: Greater Sydney costing analysis of expedited OHCA transport for possible ECPR versus standard care — overall health system costs were comparable, with higher costs when patients arrived during ECPR business hours.

papers.title: Effect of vascular access strategy on long-term outcomes in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a randomised clinical trial
papers.summary: IVIO follow-up comparing initial intraosseous versus intravenous access in adult non-traumatic OHCA — 6-month and 1-year outcomes were similar, with no evidence that either access strategy improves long-term survival or neurological outcome.

papers.title: Feasibility of portable telemedicine devices for ambulance-based prehospital triage: a comparative simulation study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Simulation study comparing portable telemedicine devices for ambulance triage, and found the Vuzix headset ranked highest overall, but the smartphone app was the most practical early implementation option.

papers.title: The Estimated Benefit of Lights and Sirens During Ambulance Transport
papers.summary: This study used a modern transport model to estimate whether lights and sirens save time, and it found a median gain of only 3.0 to 3.3 minutes per trip, which likely does not justify the known driving risks except in selected cases.

papers.id: Statewide Emergency Medical Services Protocols for
papers.title: Statewide Emergency Medical Services Protocols for Field-Initiated Blood Resuscitation
The impact of defibrillation current and pad position on return of spontaneous circulation during refractory ventricular fibrillation
papers.summary: Secondary analysis of DOSE VF examined whether transthoracic current, pad position, and ROSC were linked, and found AP pad placement delivered higher current and was independently associated with ROSC, while delivered current itself was not.

papers.title: Feasibility of portable telemedicine devices for ambulance-based prehospital triage: a comparative simulation study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Simulation study comparing portable telemedicine devices for ambulance triage, and found the Vuzix headset ranked highest overall, but the smartphone app was the most practical early implementation option.

papers.title: The diamond minutes: rethinking the earliest link of the trauma chain of survival
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Concept editorial arguing that the first minutes after injury, before EMS arrival, are a distinct high-risk window where bystander action and dispatcher guidance can prevent deaths, especially through haemorrhage control and airway management.

papers.title: Introduction of a Clinical Practice Guideline for Patella Reduction by Paramedics: The Effect on Pain Relief, Relocation, and Transport Decision
papers.summary: They tested whether Ambulance Victoria's patella-reduction guideline improved analgesia and service outcomes, and found no analgesia gain but fewer cannulae, fewer transports, and shorter cases.

papers.title: The Effect of Lights and Sirens on Critical Care Transport Time
papers.summary: They measured whether lights and sirens meaningfully shorten critical care transport, and found a statistically significant but modest time saving of about 8 minutes.

papers.title: Feasibility of a Pre-Hospital Virtual Triage and Care Model: A Mixed-Methods Pilot in Emergency Care
papers.summary: They tested a pre-hospital telehealth model for ambulance-retrieved patients, and found it was feasible, advanced senior review, and reduced ED length of stay without improving crew cycle times.

papers.title: Sonorheometry to detect traumatic induced coagulopathy during initial management of trauma patients: an observational, multi-center study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Tested whether Quantra can rapidly detect trauma-induced coagulopathy against standard lab tests, and found early Quantra analysis may reliably exclude TIC, but prospective validation is still needed.

papers.title: Chest X-Ray evaluation using GPT for tube thoracostomy or conservative care in non-tension spontaneous pneumothorax
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Tested whether a vision-enabled GPT model could estimate pneumothorax size and guide tube thoracostomy vs conservative care, and it matched radiologist measurements closely with good agreement to real-world ED decisions.

papers.title: Paramedic Patella Reduction — Ambulance Victoria CPG Evaluation
papers.summary: Retrospective study (n=1,210) evaluating whether Ambulance Victoria's Nov 2022 CPG for paramedic patella reduction changed practice — 91.8% reduction success rate, transport rate dropped 38.4%, case duration cut by ~33 minutes, and IV cannula use down 17.3%, with no change in effective analgesia rates.

papers.title: Delayed Defibrillation of Ventricular Arrhythmias During Transcutaneous Pacing
papers.summary: Case series examining the problem of ventricular arrhythmias occurring during TCP and delays to defibrillation — highlights the clinical trap of pacing artefact masking VF and the need to pause pacing to identify shockable rhythms.

papers.title: The Diamond Minutes: Rethinking the Earliest Link of the Trauma Chain of Survival
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: Concept editorial arguing that the first minutes after injury, before EMS arrival, are a distinct high-risk window where bystander action and dispatcher guidance can prevent deaths, especially through haemorrhage control and airway management.

topPicks.title: Duration of Emergency Medical Services-Initiated Prehospital Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Efforts and Survival for Pediatric Patients with Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
topPicks.authors: Masashi Okubo, Sho Komukai, Junichi Izawa, et al.
topPicks.summary: This nationwide cohort examined whether longer prehospital CPR affects survival in paediatric OHCA, finding prolonged CPR can still yield favourable outcomes in selected patients.

topPicks.title: Geographic Inequalities in Prehospital Critical Care for Cardiac Arrest: A Spatial Analysis of Deprivation and Service Configuration
